chunks: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Babawayh (the Mentioner) narrated to us, saying: I heard the great judge Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Ahmad al-Tabari say: Abu Sa'id al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Zakariya ibn Zafar al-Adawi al-Basri narrated to me, saying: I passed in Basra at the place of 'Tahhan', which is a quarter, and there was a crowd at the door, people entering a house, and people leaving, so I entered and found a sheikh saying: My master Anas ibn Malik narrated to me. - He is 'Kharash', the freedman of 'Anas' - Abu Sa'id said: I did not have paper with me, so I borrowed a pen and wrote these fourteen on the back of my sandals:

key_terms.أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلِيُّ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَ: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Babawayh, a prominent Shia scholar and narrator.
key_terms.أَبُو سَعِيدٍ الْحَسَنُ بْنُ عَلِيِّ بْن: Abu Sa'id al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Zakariya, the narrator in this chain.
key_terms.أَنَسُ بْنُ مَالِكٍ: Anas ibn Malik, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.
key_terms.الْبَصْرَةُ: Basra, a major city in Iraq known for its scholars.
key_terms.الْقَاضِي الْكَبِيرُ: The great judge, a title for a high-ranking jurist.
key_terms.خَرَّاشٌ: Kharash, the name of the freedman (mawla) of Anas ibn Malik.

ai.seo_question: How were early Shia hadiths preserved and transmitted according to the chain of Abu Sa'id al-Basri?
ai.summary: This anecdote from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Ma'ani al-Akhbar* illustrates the material conditions of early hadith transmission, where scholars like Abu Sa'id al-Qattan improvised by writing on the backs of their sandals (*al-nu'l*) when paper was scarce. It underscores the urgency and reverence with which the companions and their successors preserved the Prophet's teachings, reflecting the practical realities of the Basran scholarly milieu during the formative period of Shia and Sunni hadith sciences.
